Characteristic half-spaces and ramified roots

Written and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Public domain (CC0). No independent review is claimed.

A characteristic plane can bound the exact support of a smooth homogeneous solution. The lower terms of the operator matter: a function of the normal coordinate alone generally does not solve the equation. We construct a complex characteristic curve that accounts for every lower term, integrate its exponential solutions on an upper contour, and then move that contour to prove analyticity on the occupied side.

Throughout, , is a nonzero complex polynomial on of degree , and is its highest homogeneous part. A half-space normal is always a nonzero real vector. We prove The constructed solution extends holomorphically from the open negative half-space to . It is flat on the boundary and is not real analytic at any boundary point.

The programme inputs are scalar implicit graphs and persistent root counts, Lemma 2.1 and the root-count part of Lemma 4.1; the circle Cauchy formula and convergent local series, Corollary 2.2; polydisk Cauchy and the identity principle, Section 3; complex Green integration, including finite corners, Corollaries 2.3–2.4; and Schwartz Fourier inversion, F1–F4. The converse in (1) uses the full support-normal conclusion of analytic differential uniqueness, Corollary 4. All these readings are included in the course.

1. A bounded algebraic root becomes a convergent power series

The following finite argument is the part that allows collisions at the origin. Analytic labels on a ball with simple roots do not by themselves cover such a collision.

Lemma 1 (a ramified root through zero). Let and suppose . There are , , and a holomorphic function on , such that In particular on a smaller disk. The zero function is allowed.

Proof. We first justify the finite algebra used to remove persistent repetitions. The rational functions form a field. Over any field, division of one polynomial in by another is obtained by cancelling the highest term repeatedly; at every step the degree decreases. The successive nonzero remainders therefore terminate. Back-substituting expresses the last monic remainder as a linear combination of the two initial polynomials. It is their greatest common divisor: it divides both by the remainder equations, and every common divisor divides every remainder. Thus relatively prime polynomials have a Bézout identity.

Every nonconstant monic polynomial over a field factors into monic irreducibles, by induction on degree: a reducible polynomial splits into two smaller positive degrees. Two distinct monic irreducibles are relatively prime. An irreducible divides a product only if it divides one factor, since otherwise its Bézout identity with one factor, multiplied by the other, proves divisibility of the other. This also proves uniqueness of the irreducible factors and their multiplicities by successive cancellation.

Apply these facts over to write Here the are distinct monic irreducibles. The last identity follows because and are relatively prime. Indeed, an irreducible has nonzero derivative of smaller degree in characteristic zero. Reducing the derivative of the product modulo gives , which is not divisible by , by the preceding divisibility fact.

There are only finitely many poles among the rational coefficients in (4). Shrink to exclude every nonzero one from . On that punctured disk, and have exactly the same distinct zeros, by the factorization, and every zero of is simple, by its Bézout identity.

For clarity, the elementary complex polynomial fact used here also follows from our Cauchy input. If a nonconstant complex polynomial had no zero, its reciprocal would be entire and bounded: it tends to zero at infinity because its leading term dominates the lower terms, and it is bounded on each compact disk. Cauchy's derivative estimate on disks of radius tending to infinity makes the derivative of any bounded entire function zero. The scalar fundamental theorem of calculus along segments then makes it constant, a contradiction for that reciprocal. Removing a linear factor at each zero by polynomial division proves factorization into precisely the degree many roots with multiplicity.

Choose so that zero is the only root of in . On the compact annulus , its modulus has a positive minimum. After a further reduction of , has no zero on that annulus for . The proved root-count part of U025 Lemma 4.1 shows that the disk contains the same positive number of roots with multiplicity as at . For , these roots are among the simple roots of .

We spell out continuation because no assertion about a single-valued root on the punctured disk is being assumed. At each , U025 Lemma 2.1 gives a holomorphic graph for each simple root of . Shrink a common neighborhood until these graphs stay distinct. They exhaust the roots of the monic polynomial , by its fixed degree and factorization. The graphs inside cannot leave that disk because of the zero-free annulus. Their number is consequently locally constant and hence constant on the punctured disk, which is path connected by radial segments and circular arcs. We have .

A path in the punctured disk continues each root uniquely. To check existence along the whole path, cover its compact image by finitely many of the preceding graph neighborhoods and subdivide the path so each subpath lies in one of them. The subdivision exists by uniform continuity and the following finite-cover fact: a finite open cover of a compact metric set has a positive number such that every subset of smaller diameter lies in a cover member. Otherwise choose successively smaller failing subsets and one point in each; a convergent subsequence of these points eventually places each entire subset in a fixed open neighborhood of its limit. Within each graph neighborhood continuation is forced; uniqueness of the local implicit graph makes successive choices agree.

The final root does not change under a homotopy of paths fixing their endpoints. Cover the compact homotopy image by graph neighborhoods and subdivide its parameter square into sufficiently small rectangles. The image of each rectangle lies in one graph neighborhood by the same finite-cover fact. Continuing around its four edges returns to the same graph. Compare the routes across successive rows of rectangles; the intervening edges are traversed in opposite directions and their continuation maps cancel. The two outside paths therefore give the same endpoint. This is a finite proof of the required homotopy assertion.

Use the logarithmic parameter The preceding local graphs pull back to this half-plane. It is convex, so any two paths with the same endpoints are homotopic there by straight interpolation. Continuing the initial roots therefore gives single-valued holomorphic functions on the whole half-plane. They remain distinct: a meeting would, by reverse continuation, identify two different initial roots. Their holomorphy follows because near each point they coincide with its implicit graphs.

Translation permutes these labels. The permutation is constant on the half-plane: at any point its matching labels are separated, so continuity fixes the matching on a neighborhood, and connectedness then fixes it everywhere. Choose one label and let be the length of its permutation cycle. Then For , define using any local logarithm. These logarithms exist, for example by the convergent series for near each nonzero point; their possible values differ by times an integer, as follows from the real exponential and trigonometric parametrization of the circle. Equation (6) makes independent of the choice. It is holomorphic, bounded by , and satisfies .

Here is a direct removal of the missing point. Define off zero and . Boundedness gives continuity at zero and . Thus is complex differentiable everywhere in the disk. U013 Corollary 2.2 gives its convergent power series, whose constant and linear coefficients vanish. Dividing that series by extends holomorphically. Its value satisfies by continuity and , hence equals zero by the choice of the annulus. Its power series is (3), and its quotient by is bounded on every smaller closed disk. This proves the lemma.

The continuation and rectangular-grid mechanism is also proved for simple polynomial roots on a ball in AN-02, Regular balls, moving roots and complex gauges, Lemma 4. Here its finite argument is extended explicitly to the logarithmic half-plane, and the collision and removal at zero are proved above.

5. Nonvanishing and exact support

Theorem 5 (a solution with prescribed characteristic half-space support). Under , the function in Lemma 3 is nonzero and has exactly the support in (1).

Proof. Since are real and independent, put Then , , and . At , (14) gives The function is Schwartz and is nowhere zero. Indeed, keeps away from zero, and (13) gives stretched-exponential decay. Repeated differentiation gives a finite sum of products of powers times that exponential; induction by the product and chain rules proves this description at every fixed order. Those factors have at most polynomial growth, and the decay absorbs every polynomial, as in Lemma 3.

If were identically zero, (26) would make the inverse Fourier transform of identically zero. The two inverse identities in U017 F4 would imply , a contradiction. Thus .

By Lemma 3, on the positive half-space and, by continuity, on its boundary. Therefore some point of the negative half-space has . Lemma 4 makes real analytic throughout that connected half-space. A real analytic function on a connected open set that vanishes on a nonempty open subset vanishes everywhere. To verify the form used here, the set of points with a zero neighborhood is open. At any limit point within the domain, every derivative vanishes by continuity of the derivatives, so the convergent Taylor series gives a zero neighborhood there; the set is also closed. Connectedness proves the assertion. Consequently cannot vanish on any open subset of the negative half-space. Every such point lies in its support. The support is closed and is contained in the closed negative half-space, so it is exactly that half-space.

Corollary 6 (the equivalence and zero Cauchy data). Equation (1) holds, including degree zero. In the characteristic case, all derivatives of the constructed vanish on the boundary, but fails to be real analytic at every boundary point.

Proof. If , the equation is multiplication by a nonzero constant, so only the zero solution exists and . For , Theorem 5 proves sufficiency. Conversely, suppose a distributional solution has the stated exact support. At any point of its boundary, the real linear function supports the support from above. Thus is an exterior support normal in the definition used in U085. Corollary 4 of U087 places it in the characteristic set of , which gives .

For the smooth constructed solution, every derivative is zero in the positive half-space. Continuity of that derivative makes it zero on the boundary as well. Real analyticity at a boundary point would give a convergent Taylor series with every coefficient zero, hence a zero neighborhood crossing into the negative half-space, contradicting exact support. This proves both remaining claims.

Exercise 7 (advanced: infinitely many zero data). Explain why knowing every normal and tangential derivative on the characteristic plane does not determine a smooth solution, and why no boundary point of the constructed solution can have an analytic neighborhood.

Solution. The zero solution and the solution of Theorem 5 have all coordinate derivatives zero at every boundary point by Corollary 6. Each fixed normal or tangential derivative is a constant linear combination of coordinate derivatives, so their iterates agree as well. These are two different smooth solutions with identical data of every finite order, simultaneously. If the nonzero solution were analytic near any boundary point, its Taylor series there would be identically zero. It would vanish on a neighborhood containing negative-half-space points, which contradicts its exact support. This concerns smooth solutions; it makes no assertion that an analytic nonzero solution can have such data.

Exercise 8 (advanced: what changes for a system). Suppose several constant-coefficient polynomials vanish on the same curve satisfying (8), with real and independent. Prove the common half-space construction. Then show that a common principal characteristic normal alone is insufficient for a system.

Solution. Choose and use (14). Its convergence, independence of height, analyticity, nonvanishing and exact-support arguments involve only the curve estimate and the independence of . Applying each under the integral gives zero by its exact vanishing on the curve. Thus the same function solves the whole system. In contrast, the two equations and have the common principal symbol , which vanishes at . Subtracting the equations forces . Their full polynomials have no common zero, so there is no common curve of the required kind. The principal condition suffices for the single equation of Theorem 5, not for arbitrary systems.
